stem.text:
Determine\, algebraically\, if $f \(x \)= frac(1 ,x + 5 )$ and $g \(x \)= frac(1 ,x - 5 )$ are inverses of each other.

Justify your answer.

extensions.latexSource:
Determine, algebraically, if \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x+5}\) and \(g(x)=\frac{1}{x-5}\) are inverses of each other.

Justify your answer.

solution.text:
*Method 1: Find the inverse.*

$ y &= frac(1, x+5) \
  x &= frac(1, y+5) \
  y+5 &= frac(1, x) \
  y &= frac(1, x)-5 $

Therefore $f^(-1)(x)=frac(1,x)-5$, which is not $g(x)=frac(1,x-5)$. The functions are not inverses.

*Method 2: Check composition.*

$ f(g(x)) &= frac(1, frac(1,x-5)+5) \
         &= frac(x-5, 5x-24) $

Similarly,

$ g(f(x)) &= frac(1, frac(1,x+5)-5) \
         &= frac(x+5, -5x-24) $

Neither composition is identically $x$, confirming that the functions are not inverses.

Scoring: 1 mark for setting up the inverse or a composition; $frac(1,2)$ mark for simplification; $frac(1,2)$ mark for justification.

extensions.latexSource:
Method 1

Let \(f(x)=y\)

\[ \begin{array}{rlrl} y & =\frac{1}{x+5} & & \\ x & =\frac{1}{y+5} & & 1 \text { mark for switching } x \text { and } y \text { values } \\ y+5 & =\frac{1}{x} & & \\ y & =\frac{1}{x}-5 & & 1 / 2 \text { mark for solving for } y \\ f^{-1}(x) & =\frac{1}{x}-5 & & \\ \therefore f^{-1}(x) & \neq g(x) & 1 / 2 \text { mark for justification } \end{array} \]

2 marks

Method 2

\[ \begin{aligned} f(g(x)) & =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{x-5}\right)+5} & 1 \text { mark for } f(g(x)) \text { or } g(f(x)) & g(f(x)) \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{x+5}\right)-5} \\ & =\frac{1}{\frac{1+5 x-25}{x-5}} \\ & =\frac{1}{\frac{5 x-24}{x-5}} \\ & =\frac{x-5}{5 x-24} \end{aligned} \quad \frac{1}{x+5} \text { mark for simplification } \quad=\frac{1}{\frac{-5 x-24}{x+5}}, \quad=\frac{x+5}{-5 x-24} . \]

∴ They are not inverses because \(f(g(x)) \neq x\) or \(\mathrm{g}(f(x)) \neq x . \quad \frac{1}{2}\) mark for justification

2 marks

stem.text: Solve $cos  2  theta = 0 $\, where $theta  in  bb(R )$.

extensions.latexSource: Solve \(\cos 2 \theta=0\), where \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\).

solution.text:
*Method 1: Use the sine double-angle identity.*

$ 1-2sin^2 theta &= 0 \
  sin theta &= plus.minus frac(sqrt(2),2) $

In one full revolution, $theta=pi/4, 3pi/4, 5pi/4, 7pi/4$. Thus the general solution is

$ theta=pi/4+frac(k pi,2), quad k in ZZ. $

Equivalently, $theta=pi/4+k pi$ or $theta=3pi/4+k pi$, where $k in ZZ$.

*Method 2: Use the cosine double-angle identity.*

$ 2cos^2 theta-1 &= 0 \
  cos theta &= plus.minus frac(sqrt(2),2) $

This gives the same four values in one revolution and the same general solution.

Scoring: 1 mark for the double-angle identity; 1 mark for solving for the trigonometric ratio; 1 mark for angle values; 1 mark for the general solution. Retain both branches when taking the square root.
